items.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003
items.q: I heard this anecdote about a critic who had written about Albert Ayler

ctx.x: Do you find it difficult sometimes to let’s say reign in your own opinions about whether songs, particular songs from artists have a meaning beyond the music? And what I mean

by that, I heard this anecdote about a critic who had written about Albert Ayler and was imposing his own feelings about the music that Albert was playing about oppression and his passion and the whole thing, and that Albert read that and said, “That’s not what I was thinking at all, I was just playing.” So to shorten the question, do you ever have a circumstance where you have to say to yourself maybe this isn’t what this person was about at all?

I’ve had that circumstance but I don’t necessarily try to reign it in I just try to clue in the reader that maybe this is coming from me. I think that whatever the art suggests to the perceiver of the art is valid. At least to that perceiver it’s valid. And then we can debate about what — the interpretation is one of the things that critics or journalists, particularly critics, are supposed to be about. Interpreting the art.
